blocks.text: Both containers may share expected lookup complexity, but a set represents key presence while a map represents key-to-value association. The correct choice is the smallest state that preserves every downstream requirement. Worst-case guarantees, memory overhead, and implementation details may then influence the broader strategy, but they do not erase the semantic distinction.

messages.text: Retaining unused payloads obscures the invariant and can introduce unnecessary update policy; more capacity is not automatically a better contract.
Equal asymptotic lookup cost does not make two state representations preserve the same information.

feedback.reason: Asymptotic access cost and semantic payload are separate decisions; the output and invariant choose the state shape.

blocks.text: At the start of each iteration, the set must contain exactly the values from earlier iterations. Reporting and insertion are alternative branches: a present value ends the search, while an absent value is inserted for future iterations.

items: Query the unchanged seen set, whose members all come from earlier positions.

Otherwise, insert it and advance to the next position.

blocks.text: On a one-element input [7], insert-before-query makes 7 appear present even though no earlier occurrence exists. Query-before-insert returns no duplicate for [7] and detects the second occurrence in [7, 7].

blocks.text: Choosing a map is not enough—the update rule defines what the payload means. With write-if-absent, the invariant is that map[value] is the minimum processed index for that value. Overwrite-every-time is correct only when the latest index is required or any index is acceptable under a separately proven rule.

messages.text: Overwriting changes the payload from earliest occurrence to latest occurrence and violates the stated provenance contract.

feedback.reason: A map payload needs an explicit replacement policy; preserving the earliest index means first write wins.

blocks.text: For each processed value, the map maintains the invariant count[value] equals the number of processed occurrences. Presence is a derived condition count[value] > 0, but the reverse derivation is impossible. This distinction transfers to multisets, quotas, and threshold crossings.

Task B must retrieve the earlier position when the duplicate is encountered, so the key requires an index payload. This is the core transfer rule for set-versus-map decisions: follow the output contract, not the surface wording of the problem.

blocks.text: The set-versus-map decision is determined by what information must survive after the key is found. A set stores only existence. A map stores a payload such as count, index, or list. Multiple requirements can share the same key but require different payload types, so “use a map” is only the first part of the state decision.
